input:
Two liquids which mix only in part form two liquid phases over a certain range of overall composition, and the pair is said to be in equilibrium when a particular condition on the components is satisfied. This condition, which lies at the very heart of the subject, is stated here in words, before any equation is introduced: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in the two phases. So long as the chemical potential of a component differs between the phases, the component passes from the phase in which its potential is higher to the phase in which it is lower, and this transfer continues until the potentials become equal and the net passage duly stops.

The equality of chemical potential fixes what each phase contains. At a stated temperature and pressure, each phase takes on a definite composition, which is set by the pair and by its interactions, and neither composition moves as the overall composition of the mixture is changed. What does change, instead, is the amount of each phase. A mixture whose overall composition lies near one end of the range holds more of the phase that is rich in that component, and the proportions of the two phases follow from where the overall composition falls between the two phase compositions, which are the ends of the tie line joining them.

Temperature, for its part, moves the boundary of the range. For many pairs, the region of partial miscibility shrinks as the temperature rises, the two phase compositions approach each other ever more closely, and the phases eventually merge into one at a consolute temperature; a smaller class of pairs, by contrast, widens its region on heating. The equilibrium condition itself remains unchanged across that boundary, and it governs the single phase just as it governs the two, the equality being satisfied there by a uniform composition throughout.
